# Double-acting rotative steam engine (`rotative_steam_engine`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Deps: needs crank_connecting_rod, safety_valve_boiler; helped by separate_condenser, feedback_control, gears_gear_trains, machine_tools
- Core idea: Newcomen's pumping engine has one working stroke per cycle. A crank and flywheel can take rotary power from a single-acting engine. Watt's double-acting design delivers work on both strokes: valves admit steam to one side of the piston while connecting the other side to the condenser. The beam drives the flywheel. Since the piston now pushes as well as pulls, the chain must give way to a rigid rod guided in a straight line (Watt's parallel-motion linkage, or a crosshead in slides). Cutting off the steam early in the stroke and letting it expand saves more fuel. A centrifugal governor, two balls that fly outward as speed rises and partly close the throttle, reduces steam admission when the load falls. This is the engine that could drive a mill anywhere, independent of streams.
- Pitfalls:
  - Keeping the chain and arch head of the pumping engine; a chain cannot push
  - A light flywheel gives uneven speed. A single crank stopped at dead centre needs an external turn to start, however heavy its flywheel
  - Thinking Watt invented the crank; it was old, but James Pickard held a patent on its use with steam engines, hence Watt's sun-and-planet gear
- History: europe: 1779–1780 – Wasbrough and Pickard fit a crank and flywheel to a Newcomen engine; 1781 sun-and-planet gear (Murdoch, for Boulton and Watt); 1782 double-acting engine and expansive working patented; 1784 parallel motion; 1786 Albion Mills, London; 1788 centrifugal governor, adapted from windmills
- Read:
  - H. W. Dickinson & Rhys Jenkins, James Watt and the Steam Engine (1927)
  - Richard L. Hills, Power from Steam: A History of the Stationary Steam Engine (1989)
